extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; literary critics and scholars of eighteenth-century poetry
extracted.subtask_description: A close critical appraisal of Edward Young's poetic and prose style (especially the Night Thoughts), identifying strengths and persistent faults and using those observations as prescriptive/diagnostic criteria for good poetic practice. Useful for critics, teachers, or writers studying 18th-century didactic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic moral sentiment over interested obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: "substitutes interested obedience for sympathetic emotion, and baptizes egoism as religion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether religious/moral language springs from genuine sympathy and enlarged human feeling rather than self-interested vanity. The essay treats Young's moral tone as 'low and false' when it reads as egoistic devotion; aim for sincerity and sympathetic emotion in moral poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Pindaric bombast (furious bombast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Young's use of the Pindaric ode "helped him to surpass himself in furious bombast."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware inflated, declamatory passages that substitute grandiloquence for genuine elevation. The text cites lines like the naval-lyric exhortation ('Awake! awake! awake! awake!') as exemplars of overblown Pindarism—prefer restraint, clarity of image, and proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess the 'common-sense' of what is fitting in speech and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope: Young had 'much of a sublime genius without common-sense'—the want of 'that fine sense of what is fitting in speech and action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge work for appropriateness of tone, diction, and moral bearing to subject and occasion. A poet's genius should be tempered by taste and fitness; otherwise sublime passages misfire or seem ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray believable, particular human beings rather than abstract lay-figures
rubrics_metrics.description: "His muse never stood face to face with a genuine living human being; she would have been as much startled..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characterization: are characters concrete and individuated or merely vehicles for abstractions and didactic points? The essay criticizes Young's 'transparent shadows'—good writing should show persons who feel and act as humans, not merely exemplify ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid performative renunciations that mask continued hope for favor
rubrics_metrics.description: Young's 'ostentatious renunciation of worldly schemes... are in the tone of one who retains some hope in the midst of his querulousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for consistency between professed stance (e.g., renunciation, humility) and actual conduct or rhetorical pressure. Performative contradictions weaken authority and credibility in moral/poetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let affectation or simulated contempt betray servility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The audacity of affectation with which the most servile of poets professes to despise servility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for ironic or insincere postures—declamations that claim disdain for the world while actually currying favor. Authentic voice is preferable to theatrical anti-servility; affectation is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on antithetic apothegm and rhapsodic climax
rubrics_metrics.description: "The same appetency toward antithetic apothegm and rhapsodic climax" recurs across Young's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate variety and rhetorical balance. Repeated patterns of terse antithesis and escalating rhetorical climax become predictable and diminish impact; seek varied rhythms and modes of argument/feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against perilous juxtapositions that turn compliments into sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: "Perilous juxtaposition of ideas by which... unconsciously converts his compliments into sarcasms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test epithets and comparisons in context—novel or bold pairings can produce unintended irony. Ensure modifiers and images harmonize with intended praise or seriousness to avoid accidental sarcasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep poetic diction appropriate to form—avoid diluting poetry into prose (or vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: "His prose writings all read like the 'Night Thoughts,' either diluted into prose or not yet crystallized into poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether form and diction align: prose should not be merely diluted poetry, nor should poetry be prose in verse. Each form requires its own concentration, compression, and figures; failure to respect that produces formlessness or bathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chronological/factual alteration for effect should be recognized and handled carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: "Departing from the truth of dates, in order to heighten the effect of his calamity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the ethical and aesthetic effects when an author alters facts for emphasis. Such liberties can heighten emotional effect but may also mislead or compromise credibility; critics should mark where invention distorts history for dramatic purposes.
